newsitem.title: ITALY: Albania opens political can of worms in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Albania opens political can of worms in Italy.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi ran into more trouble on Friday over plans for an Italian-led security force in chaotic Albania when one key ally ruled out its backing and another questioned his government's future.
Prodi met Fausto Bertinotti, leader of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, for talks to try to mend the embarrassing split and head off future political problems.

But Bertinotti, whose support gives Prodi's centre-left government a parliamentary majority, told a news conference he remained opposed to the force which Italian military commanders hope to begin deploying late next week.
"We confirm our decision to vote against (the mission)," he said. Votes are due in both houses of parliament next week.

Franco Marini, leader of the centrist Popular Party which is a member of Prodi's coalition, said that the latest tensions with Communist Refoundation meant it was time to review the governing alliance to determine whether it could survive.
"I'm not looking for a crisis," he told La Repubblica newspaper. "But without a minimum of common objectives, this government won't get very far."

The government relies on support from Communist Refoundation for a majority in parliament's lower house, but it is in no immediate danger over the Albania votes because the opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance has already promised its backing.
Bertinotti, who has a fractious relationship with the government, said it was "unnecessary, useless and wrong" to suggest that he was trying to bring Prodi down.
Prodi has insisted that his government will last an unprecedented full five years and that his majority will hold.
Bertinotti played down the dissent on Albania, saying his party had split with the government in the past on major issues, such as NATO and European economic and monetary union (EMU).
But the government faces further, potentially more serious, battles with Refoundation in the months ahead on its efforts to qualify for EMU and on streamlining social spending.
Bertinotti objects to sacrifices for a single currency he thinks will not start on time and bitterly opposes welfare cuts.

Marini told reporters that if Prodi fell, it might be possible for a minority government, which would have to rely on support from the Freedom Alliance, to stay in office to oversee Italy's goal of becoming a founder member of EMU in 1999.
His words put him at odds with the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left, the biggest in Prodi's government, which says a government fall would lead to an early general election.
Prodi's government, which is due to celebrate its first birthday next month, is Italy's 55th since World War Two.
The Albania force, which will secure transport links to deliver relief following last month's armed anarchy, has been approved by the U.N. Security Council.
An opinion poll published on Friday by the Datamedia group showed 69.3 percent of Italians backed the mission.
